content.title: About
content.content: Carp is a freshwater fish of the family Cyprinidae, widely found in rivers and lakes across Europe and Asia. It has firm flesh, a mildly sweet flavor, and distinctive large scales. Carp is used in both traditional and modern cuisines.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Carp can grow over 1.5 m in length and weigh more than 30 kg.
In some cultures carp is a symbol of luck and is featured in New Year dishes.
Carp can survive low‑oxygen conditions by breathing through its skin.
Aquaculture farms raise carp in intensive systems to provide a steady supply.
Male carp develop bright red breeding tubercles during the spawning season.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Carp meat provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: The fish contains polyunsaturated fats that support heart and vascular health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Carp supplies vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, which aid energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: It offers phosphorus, selenium, and potassium, important for bones, antioxidant protection, and blood pressure regulation.

items.title: Low mercury content
items.content: Compared with many marine fish, carp typically contains less mercury, making it a safer choice.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to fish, including carp.

items.title: Parasite contamination
items.content: Raw or undercooked carp can harbor parasites; proper cooking is recommended.

items.title: High sodium in cured preparations
items.content: Traditional methods such as salting or smoking can increase the salt content.

items.title: Environmental concerns
items.content: Intensive carp farming may affect water quality and biodiversity.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Carp is commonly baked, fried, boiled, or made into fish cakes. Fillets can be added to salads, soups, and stews. When cooking, it is important to remove bones and skin.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh carp should be kept in the refrigerator at 0‑2 °C for no more than 2 days. Frozen carp can be stored at –18 °C for up to 6 months. Before cooking, rinse and pat the fish dry.

content.title: About
content.content: Garlic bread is a fragrant loaf, usually made from a baguette or ciabatta, brushed with a mixture of butter, minced garlic, herbs, and sometimes cheese. It is popular as a snack or side dish for soups, pasta, and salads.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Garlic bread is often served in Italian restaurants alongside pasta.
There are many variations, including versions with Parmesan, mozzarella, or spicy herbs.
Garlic enhances flavor perception and has antibacterial properties.
The traditional recipe calls for baking the bread until the crust turns golden.
In some countries, garlic bread is served as small bite‑size pieces called “grissini.”

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Garlic contains allicin and other compounds that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Regular consumption of garlic may strengthen the immune system.

items.title: Cholesterol reduction
items.content: Studies suggest garlic can help lower “bad” LDL cholesterol levels.

items.title: Improved digestion
items.content: Garlic stimulates gastric juice production, aiding nutrient absorption.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: It provides vitamin B6, important for protein metabolism.

items.title: Garlic allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions such as swelling or rash.

items.title: Stomach irritation
items.content: Large amounts of raw garlic can cause heartburn or discomfort.

items.title: Breath odor
items.content: Garlic breath can linger for several hours after eating.

items.title: Interaction with medications
items.content: Garlic may enhance the effect of anticoagulants, so caution is advised for those on blood thinners.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice a baguette, spread a mixture of butter, minced garlic, and herbs, then bake until golden. Serve hot, cutting into serving pieces. Optionally sprinkle grated cheese a few minutes before the end of baking.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Best consumed within 1‑2 days. Keep in an airtight container at room temperature to retain crust crispness. For longer storage, freeze in bags and reheat in the oven before serving.

grapefruit-juice-100-canned-bottled-or-i.title: Grapefruit juice, 100 %, canned, bottled or in a carton

content.title: About
content.content: 100 % grapefruit juice is obtained from ripe grapefruits without added sugar, preservatives or flavorings. It is sold in cans, glass bottles and carton packs. The juice has a characteristic sweet‑tart taste, bright aroma and a high vitamin C content.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Grapefruit was created in the Caribbean in the early 19th century as a hybrid of pomelo and sweet orange.
The juice is widely used in marinades, sauces and cocktails.
Its vivid colour and flavour make it a natural food colourant in many products.
In the United States grapefruit juice is one of the most popular non‑alcoholic summer drinks.
Pasteurisation retains most nutrients, although some enzymes may be lost.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: A 100 ml serving provides about 30 mg of vitamin C, which supports immunity and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Flavonoids such as naringenin and hesperidin help neutralise free radicals.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Acids in the juice stimulate gastric juice production, aiding food digestion.

items.title: May lower cholesterol
items.content: Studies suggest regular consumption can help reduce LDL‑cholesterol levels.

items.title: Aids weight control
items.content: Low in calories (≈ 40 kcal per 100 ml) and provides a feeling of fullness, making it suitable for diet plans.

items.title: Drug interactions
items.content: Grapefruit can increase the effect of certain medicines (e.g., statins, antihistamines); consult a doctor if you take medication.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: High acidity may irritate the stomach lining in people with gastritis or ulcers.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to citrus.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Even without added sugar, natural sugars can affect blood glucose levels in diabetics.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Drink it chilled as a refreshing beverage, use it in smoothies, cocktails, marinades, sauces and desserts. It can be diluted with water to reduce acidity if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. Once opened, keep refrigerated and consume within 3–5 days. Discard if the smell or taste changes.

content.title: About
content.content: Pan dulce is a traditional Mexican sweet bread, a soft, lightly sweet roll often enriched with raisins, candied fruit, or nuts. It is popular as a breakfast or snack and is usually enjoyed with coffee or hot chocolate.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pan dulce comes in many regional shapes: conchas, cuernitos, empanadas, and more.
The dough is traditionally leavened with yeast, sugar, butter, and milk, giving it a tender crumb.
In Mexico, pan dulce is sold in bakeries (panaderías) and by street vendors in small portions.
The name literally means “sweet bread,” but in Mexican cuisine it denotes a distinct category of pastries separate from cakes and cookies.
Some regional recipes add spices such as cinnamon or anise for extra aroma.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: The carbohydrates provide quick energy, making pan dulce a convenient snack.

items.title: Contains modest protein
items.content: Milk and eggs in the recipe contribute a small amount of animal protein.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Yeast‑leavened dough supplies B1, B2, and B3 vitamins that support metabolism.

items.title: Calcium and phosphorus
items.content: Dairy ingredients add calcium and phosphorus, important for bone health.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Pan dulce is sweet, so people with diabetes or those limiting sugar should consume it in moderation.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The traditional recipe uses wheat flour, making it unsuitable for those with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Saturated fat
items.content: Butter raises the saturated fat level, which may be a concern for cardiovascular health.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pan dulce is typically eaten fresh, split in half and spread with butter, jam, or honey. It can also be added to yogurt, oatmeal, or used as a base for dessert sandwiches.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store pan dulce in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days. For longer storage keep it refrigerated (up to 7 days) or freeze it wrapped in plastic film.

content.title: About
content.content: The dry mix for scalloped potatoes contains powdered potato, dried dairy ingredients, spices and thickeners. When reconstituted with water and baked, it yields a creamy casserole ready in 30‑40 minutes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Dry mixes allow cooking without fresh ingredients, ideal for camping or time‑pressed meals.
The blend is often fortified with B‑vitamins and iron to offset nutrient loss during drying.
Traditional recipes use butter, but the dry version replaces it with powdered dairy.
Scalloped potato mix is popular in cold‑climate regions where fresh produce storage is limited.
The mix can be adapted for vegetarian and gluten‑free diets.

items.title: Carbohydrate source
items.content: Potato base provides complex carbs for quick energy.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Fortification supplies thiamine and niacin, supporting metabolism.

items.title: Potassium
items.content: Potatoes are rich in potassium, which helps maintain healthy blood pressure.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: Compared with traditional casseroles, the dry mix contains minimal fat unless additional butter is added.

items.title: Convenience and time saving
items.content: Fast preparation preserves more nutrients than prolonged cooking.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: The mix may be high in salt; people with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Contains dairy powder and possibly gluten; check the label if you have allergies.

items.title: Texture issues
items.content: Incorrect water ratio can result in a dry or overly watery casserole.

items.title: Additive content
items.content: Some mixes include flavor enhancers and preservatives that may be undesirable for sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Combine the mix with hot water (or milk), stir, pour into a baking dish and bake until golden. Optional additions include fresh vegetables, cheese, or herbs for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the dry mix in a sealed container in a cool, dry place away from moisture and direct sunlight. After opening, use within 3‑6 months.
